issues.legal_issue: The doctrine of cy-près does not govern rehabilitation allotments sought for property belonging to an institution displaced across the border.
material_facts: The appellant sought land in India in lieu of land said to have belonged to an institution left across the border.
The appellant argued in the High Court that the institution could be established at a new place and its former property attached to the new institution under the doctrine of cy-près.
The High Court rejected that argument, and the Supreme Court considered the doctrine misconceived in the context of displaced-person rehabilitation.
issues.conclusion: The doctrine of cy-près was rightly rejected as inapplicable to the rehabilitation claim.
issues.legal_principle: The law of rehabilitation of displaced persons does not apply the doctrine of cy-près to transfer property attached to an institution left across the border to an institution established at a new place. The Court referred to Samadh Parshotam Dass v. Union of India and the related appeal in which it had been stated that samadhs could not be shifted and therefore could not receive allotments in lieu of land across the border.

predicates.displaced_person_rehabilitation_proceedi: A person seeks rehabilitation through an allotment in lieu of property left across a border.
predicates.institution_property_claim: The property for which an allotment is sought is claimed as property belonging to an institution.
predicates.cy_pres_relied_on: The claimant relies on the doctrine of cy-près to support transferring the former institution's property to an institution established at a new place.
predicates.cy_pres_does_not_govern_rehabilitation_a: The doctrine of cy-près does not govern the claimed rehabilitation allotment.

issues.definition: When a displaced-person rehabilitation proceeding concerns institution property and the claimant relies on cy-près, the rule is that cy-près does not govern the rehabilitation allotment.

issues.legal_issue: A distinct ground omitted in the court below cannot be revived for the first time in an appeal.
material_facts: The appeal followed dismissal of a writ petition challenging cancellation of a land allotment.

In the High Court, the appellant relied on the doctrine of cy-près but did not argue that the institution had been re-established in India or distinguish the institution's land from land recorded in the Mahant's name.
Those distinct arguments were advanced in the Supreme Court, but had not been raised or preserved in the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The appellant could not revive those grounds for the first time in the Supreme Court, and the appeal failed.
issues.legal_principle: A party that does not raise a distinct ground in the court below loses the opportunity to raise it for the first time on appeal. The Court applied that principle to the arguments distinguishing the institution's property from land recorded in the Mahant's name and asserting that the institution had been re-established in India.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_dismissal: A party brings an appeal after a court has dismissed its writ petition.
predicates.distinct_ground_not_raised_below: The party does not raise a distinct ground in the court that decided the writ petition.
predicates.ground_cannot_be_raised_for_first_time_o: The party cannot raise that ground for the first time in the appeal.

issues.definition: When an appeal follows dismissal of a writ petition and a distinct ground was not raised below, the rule is that the ground cannot be raised for the first time on appeal.
